articles.title: Calgary man pleads guilty to threatening to kill the prime minister and his family
articles.dek: A 31-year-old Calgary man admitted to posting online threats against Prime Minister Mark Carney, along with charges tied to an attack on a tire shop.
body: A 31-year-old Calgary man pleaded guilty in a Calgary courtroom on Friday, November 20, to threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney and members of his family, The Canadian Press reported [1].

Jamie Dacosta pleaded guilty to four criminal charges [1]. Along with the threat against the prime minister, he admitted to uttering threats, extortion and mischief involving a Calgary tire shop and its staff, where video shows him smashing windows with an axe, according to the report [1].

The threats against Carney were made in online posts, including videos on YouTube and TikTok [1]. Calgary police and the RCMP's Integrated National Security Enforcement Team learned of a threat posted on YouTube, and Dacosta was arrested in September [1]. The report says Calgary police had warned him in March after a TikTok video in which he said he would harm the prime minister and kill one of his children [1]. His last post came a few days before Carney was scheduled to visit Red Deer, north of Calgary [1].
The videos were played in court, and the report says Dacosta yawned and laughed while they were shown [1].

Defence lawyer Adriano Iovinelli asked the court to order a pre-sentence report [1]. He described the comments as alarming, said his client had made clear the posts were his own, and suggested his client should be assessed for mental illness [1]. No Crown position on sentence was reported [1].

No sentencing date has been set. The case returns to court on February 4, and the Crown has time to find out whether the prime minister wishes to provide a victim impact statement, according to the report [1].
key_facts: Pleaded guilty Friday, Nov. 20, to four criminal charges
Threats were posted on YouTube and TikTok; arrest came in September
Charges also cover threats, extortion and mischief at a tire shop
Case returns to court Feb. 4; defence asked for a pre-sentence report

articles.title: Calgary Transit moving its whole bus fleet to all-weather tires after a pilot cut stuck buses by 45 per cent
articles.dek: About half of Calgary's 40- and 60-foot buses already run on all-weather tires, and the rest are due to switch by the end of 2027.
body: Calgary Transit says fewer of its buses should get stuck on snowy roads this winter, after a pilot found all-weather tires sharply reduced traction problems [1].

Last winter, the agency compared 11 buses fitted with all-season tires against 11 fitted with all-weather tires, running on routes with known winter trouble spots [1]. Buses on all-weather tires had 45 per cent fewer stuck-bus incidents [1].
Calgary Transit said that during one four-day stretch with more than 10 centimetres of snow, 100 buses got stuck across the fleet, and the units with all-weather tires got stuck less often [1].

About half of the 40- and 60-foot bus fleet, roughly 500 buses, now runs on all-weather tires, and the whole fleet is expected to have them by the end of 2027 [1]. The agency began replacing worn or damaged all-season tires with all-weather tires last year [1]. It says the approach avoids extra spending on second sets of tires, seasonal changeovers, storage and inventory, since the buses do not need to swap tires each season [1].

Calgary Transit also listed other winter measures. Routes with traction trouble spots get priority for snow clearing under The City's Priority Snow Plan, and the longer 60-foot articulated buses are limited in snowy conditions [1].
key_facts: Pilot: 11 buses on all-weather tires vs 11 on all-season tires
45% fewer stuck-bus incidents with all-weather tires
About 500 buses, roughly half the fleet, already switched
Full fleet expected on all-weather tires by end of 2027

articles.title: Alberta opens $250-million round to build more than 2,000 affordable homes
articles.dek: Housing providers across the province, including in Calgary, can apply until January 31, 2027, for help covering up to one-third of project costs.
body: The Alberta government announced on Friday, November 20, that it is committing $250 million to a new round of its Affordable Housing Partnership Program, with the aim of building more than 2,000 new affordable homes [1].

The round is open now and applications close January 31, 2027 [1]. Public, non-profit and private-sector housing providers can apply for projects that build, buy, convert or expand housing [1]. Provincial support can cover up to one-third of eligible project costs, and at least 10 per cent of units in each project must be accessible [1].

The program launched in 2022 under Stronger Foundations, the province's 10-year affordable housing plan [1]. The province says about $730 million has been committed through the program so far, for more than 7,400 new affordable homes and more than 630 shelter spaces [1].

The government says it is more than 70 per cent of the way to the plan's goal of serving 25,000 additional households by 2031, which it describes as ahead of schedule [1]. It also says about 64,500 affordable housing units are supported across Alberta, helping about 122,000 people, and that it has put $2 billion in capital funding into affordable housing, seniors housing and continuing care spaces since 2019 [1].

The release was issued by Assisted Living and Social Services Minister Nathan Neudorf's ministry [1]. It does not say how much of the new round is expected to go to Calgary projects; funding is awarded through applications from providers [1].
key_facts: $250 million for more than 2,000 affordable homes
Applications close Jan. 31, 2027
Province covers up to one-third of eligible costs
About $730 million committed through the program since 2022

articles.title: Alberta signs air deal with Discover Airlines for Edmonton-Frankfurt flight, backing Calgary service too
articles.dek: The province says the partnership supports continued Frankfurt-Calgary flights as it courts German visitors, who spent $141 million in Alberta in 2025.
body: The Alberta government, through Travel Alberta, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Lufthansa Group for a new non-stop flight between Frankfurt and Edmonton, the province announced on Friday, November 20 [1].

According to the province, the partnership will also support continued service between Frankfurt and Calgary International Airport [1]. Travel Alberta and Discover Airlines will market Alberta together to travellers in Germany [1]. The release does not give a start date for the Edmonton flight [1].

The province says visitor spending from Germany rose 12 per cent in 2025 to $141 million, with 94,000 visits [1]. It says Travel Alberta's air access investments from 2022 to 2026 supported 1.5 million additional airline seats and generated more than $13 in visitor spending for every dollar invested [1].

The agreement is tied to the government's goal of growing annual visitor spending in Alberta to $25 billion by 2035 [1]. The announcement was made by Tourism and Sport Minister Andrew Boitchenko's ministry, with comments from Travel Alberta president and CEO David Goldstein and Rupert Kraus, head of networks and partnerships at Discover Airlines [1].
key_facts: MOU with Lufthansa Group for a non-stop Frankfurt-Edmonton flight
Partnership supports continued Frankfurt-Calgary service
German visitor spending rose 12% in 2025 to $141 million
94,000 visits from Germany in 2025

articles.title: University of Calgary study calls for round-the-clock family access in children's intensive care
articles.dek: Researchers led by an Alberta Children's Hospital nurse-scientist say limits on family visits in pediatric ICUs can harm patients and families.
body: New research from a University of Calgary program recommends that children in pediatric intensive care units have access to two designated support people at all hours, LiveWire Calgary reported on November 20 [1].

The study, published earlier this month in JAMA Network Open, drew on surveys and interviews with 43 people from across Canada, including former patients, family members, clinicians and policymakers [1]. Pediatric ICUs treat patients from infancy to age 18 [1].

The work was led by Laurie Lee, an associate professor of nursing at the University of Calgary and director of the Alberta Children's Hospital PICU Research Program, with co-author Jennifer Foster of Dalhousie University [1]. The two began the research during the COVID-19 pandemic, when restrictions on family presence in intensive care units took effect [1]. It follows an earlier University of Calgary study on family togetherness for adult patients [1].

According to the report, participants said family presence helped patients, families and health-care workers, including with coping, healing and shorter stays [1]. Lee told LiveWire that having families at the bedside actually decreases workload for staff [1]. Families described limits on visiting hours and on the number of visitors, which Lee said were harmful to both patients and families [1].
The research did not support the idea that limiting contact between members of the same household reduced the spread of infectious disease, according to the report [1].

The authors recommend that patients and families help write visiting policies [1]. Hospital boards usually set these guidelines, though provincial or federal governments can override them during a health emergency [1]. The researchers plan to present their findings to policymakers at the Children's Healthcare Canada conference in April 2027 [1].
key_facts: Study surveyed and interviewed 43 people across Canada
Recommends 24/7 access for two designated support people
Published in JAMA Network Open in November 2026
Findings to be presented at a national conference in April 2027
